notes.meaning: Job begins his reply to Eliphaz. He speaks up because the speeches of his friends have given him no real help.

Job tells his friends that their speeches are old news and completely unhelpful. Instead of easing his pain, their harsh words only pile on more grief. They came to comfort him, but they act like bad physicians who make the illness worse.

Job asks when their empty, windy speeches will finally come to an end. He throws their own insults back at them, asking what provokes them to keep arguing. Their repeated claims do nothing to bring the truth to light.
Job points out that if their roles were reversed, he could easily do what they are doing. It is easy to pile up critical speeches and shake one's head in mockery at someone who is already suffering.

Instead of kicking them when they were down, Job says he would have used his words to strengthen them. True comfort tries to lighten a person's load and lift a sinking spirit rather than make pain worse.
Job feels trapped because neither speaking nor staying silent brings him any relief. If he defends himself, his friends accuse him of anger, but if he stays quiet, his pain still does not leave him.
Job turns toward God, stating that God has worn out all his strength. His family and household have been destroyed, leaving him lonely and isolated in his sorrow.

God has bound Job with severe illness, leaving his body withered and shrunken to skin and bones. His friends treat his ruined physical condition as visible proof that he must be guilty of great secret sins.
Job describes an attacker who tears into him like a wild beast and glares at him with furious eyes. In his deep sorrow, Job feels as though God Himself has turned against him as an enemy.

differ.view: Some Methodists believe the fierce enemy tearing at Job is Satan, whom God allowed to visibly terrify him.

notes.meaning: People around Job open their mouths to mock him and treat him with utter contempt. They band together against him in his misery, picturing the way Jesus Christ would later be mocked and struck by hostile crowds.

Job recognizes that God has handed him over to cruel, wicked people who mistreat him. God allowed these enemies to have power over him, just as Jesus was later delivered into the hands of sinners by God's purpose.

Job had lived in peace and security, but God shattered his comfortable life without warning. He pictures God as a powerful wrestler who grabs him by the neck, shakes him to pieces, and sets him up as an archer's target.
Arrows strike Job from every side, piercing his most vital inner parts without mercy. The spilling of his gall on the ground pictures a fatal wound that drains away his very life.
Job feels like a walled city being battered again and again until the walls collapse. God attacks him like a mighty warrior charging through the broken gaps.

Job shows the depth of his mourning by sewing rough sackcloth directly onto his wounded skin. He has laid his horn, a common picture of power and dignity, down in the dust to show complete humiliation.
Constant weeping has left Job's face flushed and swollen, and dark shadows cover his eyes. His sight is fading from grief, and he feels the darkness of death drawing near.
Even with death approaching, Job insists he is innocent of violence, fraud, and oppression. His prayers to God were sincere and pure, not the empty words of a hypocrite.
Job asks the earth not to cover his shed blood, echoing how Abel's blood cried out from the ground. He wants his suffering and unfair death to remain in plain sight until justice is done.
Job looks past his human accusers and declares that he has a witness in heaven who knows the truth. Even while feeling struck down on earth, he trusts that God in heaven knows his integrity.

differ.view: Some evangelicals see this heavenly witness and advocate as a direct pointer to Jesus Christ, who speaks to the Father on our behalf.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Pope Gregory the Great taught that anyone who possesses this witness of a clean life in heaven has no reason to fear the judgments of earthly men.

notes.meaning: Job's earthly friends offer only mockery, so he turns his tearful eyes directly to God. Earthly sympathy has failed him, but he knows God sees his tears and values a broken heart.
Job longs for someone to plead a person's case before God, just as a neighbor speaks up for a friend. He appeals from God's present anger to God's ultimate justice and mercy.

differ.view: Some Baptists see an early promise of the Messiah here, taking the phrase 'Son of man' to mean Christ pleading for His people before God.
Some Presbyterians take this as Job simply wishing he could present his own defense directly to God as one man does with another.

notes.meaning: Job knows that only a few numbered years, or short days, remain for him on earth. Soon he will travel the path of death, a journey from which no one returns to this earthly life.
